reading.translation:
During the night Xenophon slept a little. He saw a dream: fire appeared around his father’s house. On waking, he considered the dream.

The light gave him hope, but the fire gave him fear. Xenophon did not receive a certain promise of survival. He reasoned about the danger.

Then he got up and summoned Proxenus’s captains. The captains came together. Xenophon began a speech to them.

Xenophon took thought for the soldiers. “We must prepare,” he said. After hearing and considering, the captains accepted the proposal.

After summoning the other leaders too, the captains held a council. Many deliberated about survival. Xenophon did not act alone.

The officers chose new generals. Xenophon became a general in Proxenus’s place. Other men too took command: survival is a shared task.

In a different account Socrates questions Euthydemus about courage. A person ignorant of danger is not courageous for that reason. The courageous person must understand dangers.

blocks.title: Calling, considering, accepting
body: καλέω brings officers together; σκέπτομαι and λογίζομαι describe consideration and reasoning. Their aorists ἐκάλεσεν, ἐσκέψατο, and ἐλογίσατο mark actions in the narrative, rather than portraying initiative as an unexplained burst of confidence.

δέχομαι can mean receive or accept. Here ἐδέξαντο τὴν βουλήν means the captains accepted a proposal. Its middle form is translated with an active English verb; the captains are not being accepted by someone else.

κοινός means shared, and μόνος means alone. The clause οὐ μόνος ὁ Ξενοφῶν ἔπραξεν prevents an exaggerated claim of sole leadership. The separate Socratic comparison asks whether understanding danger is necessary for ἀνδρεία.

sections.title: 1. Sigmatic first aorist: active and middle
body: A regular sigmatic first aorist adds σ to the verbal stem, usually with α in the endings. λύω gives ἔλυσα, “I released,” and middle ἐλυσάμην. Past indicative augment is added before the stem just as in the second aorist.

The active endings are -σα, -σας, -σε(ν), -σαμεν, -σατε, -σαν when stated together with σ. Third singular has ε rather than α: ἔλυσε(ν). The middle pattern includes ἐλύσω, whose -ω contrasts with second-aorist middle ἐλάβου.

In ἐδέξαντο, “they accepted,” δέχομαι supplies a first-aorist middle, with χ + σ becoming ξ. Its active English meaning is learned with the verb. An ending identifies person and voice form; it does not force an English passive translation.

sections.title: 2. Consonant changes and vowel lengthening
body: Adding σ to a consonant stem produces regular spelling changes: labials π, β, φ + σ yield ψ; velars κ, γ, χ + σ yield ξ; dental sounds τ, δ, θ disappear before σ. Thus πέμπω → ἔπεμψα, πράττω → ἔπραξα, and πείθω → ἔπεισα.

A present spelling may conceal the consonant stem: πράττω belongs to a velar stem and forms πραξ-. σκέπτομαι gives ἐσκεψάμην. Learn the actual principal part together with the rule, because the present stem alone is not always a transparent guide.

Contract verbs commonly lengthen their stem vowel before σ: τιμάω → ἐτίμησα, ποιέω → ἐποίησα, δηλόω → ἐδήλωσα. This lengthening occurs inside the aorist stem and is different from temporal augment at the beginning. καλέω → ἐκάλεσα is a learned exception to automatic ε → η.

checks.answer: ψ. A labial before σ combines as ψ.
ξ. A velar before σ combines as ξ.

sections.title: 3. Active and middle first-aorist participles
body: The active first-aorist participle has λύσας, λύσασα, λῦσαν. It lacks augment. Its masculine and neuter stem contains -σαντ-: genitive λύσαντος. The feminine follows first-declension λύσασα, λυσάσης. Accent and agreement must be read together.

The middle forms are λυσάμενος, λυσαμένη, λυσάμενον. Their -άμενος ending differs from second-aorist λαβόμενος. In the reading, σκεψάμενοι describes the captains considering before accepting the proposal, and ἀκούσαντες supplies their prior hearing.

Participles agree in case, number, and gender with their head noun. καλέσαντες οἱ λοχαγοί means “the captains, having summoned ...”; καλέσαντα τὸν λοχαγόν would describe one captain as an accusative object. The participle’s aorist aspect presents its action as a whole.

examples.english: Having heard and considered, the captains accepted the proposal.

sections.title: 4. First and second aorists share aorist aspect
body: “First” and “second” name formation patterns, not the order in which events occurred. First aorist ἔλυσα has σ and α-based endings; second aorist ἔλαβον has a thematic ο/ε pattern and its own stem. Both present an action as a whole.

Compare active participles λύσας and λαβών, middle participles λυσάμενος and λαβόμενος, and infinitives λῦσαι and λαβεῖν. Each pair differs in morphological pattern. The aorist versus present distinction concerns aspect; first versus second does not.

A dictionary generally assigns the aorist actually used for a given verb and meaning. Do not invent ἔλαμψα as an aorist of λαμβάνω or append σ to every present stem. The reading’s ἀνέστη is an athematic aorist, explicitly glossed rather than an assessed formation target.

sections.title: A dream with two possible readings
body: Xenophon reports a dream of fire and describes both encouragement and anxiety in interpreting it. The light can suggest help, while the surrounding fire can suggest entrapment in the king’s territory. The narrative gives his uncertainty a place in the account.

We should describe this as a reported dream and interpretation. It supplies neither an independently verified divine promise nor permission to erase his fear. His next acts are practical: summon officers, discuss the danger, and begin organizing a response.

sections.title: Replacement command is collective
body: Xenophon first calls Proxenus’s captains, then the consultation reaches surviving commanders from other units. Cheirisophus also speaks and presses for prompt elections. The source depicts a process involving several officers rather than one man assuming absolute control.

Xenophon is chosen in Proxenus’s place; four other named replacements are selected for the other missing generals. “Xenophon became a general” is accurate. “Xenophon became the army’s sole leader” would distort the distributed command and its shared responsibilities.

sections.title: Socrates and informed courage
body: In the separate Memorabilia 4.6 discussion, Socrates questions Euthydemus about courage. Ignorance of danger does not make someone courageous simply by removing fear. Knowledge and sound response matter to the ethical definition being explored.

This is a comparison between Xenophon’s works, not a claim that the officers studied a later book during the crisis. It helps us evaluate the expedition’s decisions: getting up and speaking are valuable when they begin informed action for others, not merely a performance of confidence.
